case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the ATF’s “Frame or Receiver” Final Rule can lawfully treat certain partially complete firearm components and related kits as “firearms” under the Gun Control Act, and (procedurally) whether the Supreme Court’s interim stay order halted the district court’s judgment only to the extent it vacated the rule.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Gun Control Act of 1968 (definition of “firearm,” including “frame or receiver,” 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3)) and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) remedial authority implicated by vacatur, 5 U.S.C. §§ 706(2) and 705 (as relevant to setting aside agency action and stays).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The federal government (Garland/ATF) argues the Final Rule is a permissible interpretation and implementation of the Gun Control Act’s definition of “firearm,” allowing ATF to regulate items that functionally are or are readily convertible into frames/receivers (including certain weapon-parts kits), and that the lower courts erred by reading the statute too narrowly and by invalidating the rule; relatedly, the government has sought to preserve the rule’s operation pending review, including through a stay of the district court’s vacatur remedy.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The private challengers (VanDerStok et al.) argue ATF exceeded its statutory authority because the Gun Control Act’s text covers completed frames/receivers (and completed firearms), not unfinished parts or aggregations of parts sold as kits; therefore the Final Rule is contrary to law under the APA and must be set aside, and any interim relief should not be read to broadly suspend all aspects of the district court’s judgment beyond the vacatur portion (as indicated by the Supreme Court’s use of limiting language like “insofar as”).
key_precedents: Garland v. VanDerStok, No. 23A82, 2023 WL 5023383 (U.S. Aug. 8, 2023) (mem.)
Danco Laboratories, LLC v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 143 S. Ct. 1075 (2023) (mem.)
Pub. Serv. Co. of Ind. v. EPA, 682 F.2d 626 (7th Cir. 1982)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas press the strongest objection: that § 921(a)(3)(A)’s “may readily be converted” modifies “weapon,” not “frame or receiver,” and that ATF cannot graft a “readily convertible frame/receiver” concept onto § 921(a)(3)(B). I agree that point counsels against reading (B) itself to sweep in unfinished components, but it does not defeat a narrower, text-grounded approach—urged by Justice Alito and Justice Barrett—that integrated kits and near-complete units sold as a coherent firearm-package can qualify as a “weapon … designed to or may readily be converted” under (A) without collapsing (B) into a boundless parts regime. Thompson/Center Arms, as Justice Sotomayor notes, supports looking to configuration and predictable completion in assessing whether an aggregation is functionally a regulated firearm; while not a license for agency rewriting, it reinforces that Congress’s definition targets practical evasion, so long as we cabin today’s holding to objective, readily-completable kits rather than remote components. Given the criminal-law and lenity concerns flagged by Justice Gorsuch, the opinion should expressly reserve harder marginal cases and avoid endorsing an agency power to regulate generic parts untethered to a readily convertible “weapon” as defined in (A).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I have considered Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s effort to relocate the Rule’s coverage to § 921(a)(3)(A)’s “weapon … may readily be converted” clause for integrated kits, but that argument still cannot salvage the regulation because ATF’s Final Rule does not merely treat some packages as “weapons”; it also redefines “frame or receiver” in § 921(a)(3)(B) to reach partially complete units—an addition Congress did not enact. Justice Kagan’s “gap-filling” point (undefined “frame or receiver”) fails under textualism because we supply the ordinary public meaning at enactment and do not permit an agency to expand a criminally operative definition under the guise of line-drawing, especially where any real uncertainty is resolved by lenity. Justice Sotomayor’s invocation of Thompson/Center Arms does not move me: that case’s distinct NFA context and its focus on whether an aggregation constituted a regulated “weapon” cannot authorize ATF to rewrite the separate GCA category of “the frame or receiver” into a “readily convertible” receiver. Even if some kits might fit within (A) in particular applications, the Rule’s broader definitional rewrite exceeds the statute’s text, so I remain with the Respondent.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s best point is that § 921(a)(3)(A)’s “may readily be converted” modifies “weapon,” not “frame or receiver,” and that lenity cautions against stretching a criminal definition. But I think Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett are right that the statute’s structure already supplies the limiting principle: when a seller markets and packages an integrated kit as a coherent weapon-in-waiting that is objectively “readily” completed, it fits within “any weapon … designed to or may readily be converted” without redefining § 921(a)(3)(B). Justice Thomas is correct to resist ATF “adding” a readily-convertible gloss to “frame or receiver,” yet his approach would create an administrable loophole precisely where Congress used forward-looking language to prevent evasion, and that is not a grievous ambiguity calling for lenity. Thompson/Center Arms, as Justice Sotomayor notes, reinforces that we can look to configuration and predictable, intended assembly to identify the regulated “weapon,” while still rejecting an untethered parts-regulation theory.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s best point is that § 921(a)(3)(A)’s “may readily be converted” modifies “weapon,” not “frame or receiver,” and that lenity counsels against agency expansion in a criminally consequential definition. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the statute’s integrated structure and anti-evasion function make it textually coherent to treat objectively, near-complete kits marketed and configured for prompt completion as “weapons … designed to or may readily be converted,” without rewriting § 921(a)(3)(B) into a free-floating “readily convertible receiver” category. Justice Thomas’s at-enactment meaning argument underestimates how Congress deliberately used functional language to reach firearms-in-waiting; Thompson/Center Arms supports focusing on real-world configuration and intended use where conversion is straightforward, which is exactly how these kits operate. Given the predictable public-safety burdens of a loophole-driven reading, I would uphold the Rule at least as applied to integrated kits/near-complete items under (A), while insisting on clear, objective limits to address notice and avoid sweeping in remote parts.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas press the best textual point: § 921(a)(3)(B)’s separate listing of “frame or receiver” suggests Congress had a distinct object in mind and did not expressly add a “readily convertible frame/receiver” category, with lenity as a backstop. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett that the statutory definition must be read as a coherent whole: § 921(a)(3)(A) expressly reaches items “designed to” or that “may readily be converted” into functional weapons, and that text can cover integrated kits and near-complete configurations without collapsing (B) into an unbounded parts regime. Thompson/Center Arms, as Justice Sotomayor notes, reinforces that we may look at configuration/aggregation to prevent obvious evasion when conversion is straightforward, while still insisting on objective limiting principles (the “readily” factors) to avoid sweeping in remote, early-stage materials. Because this can be resolved through a narrow, text-tethered construction that preserves notice and avoids rewriting (B), I do not think the Respondent’s ordinary-meaning/lenity arguments genuinely undermine the Petitioner’s position.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s effort to uphold the Rule “narrowly” by routing kits through § 921(a)(3)(A)’s “may readily be converted” language (and Justice Alito’s similar move) is the strongest point for the government, but it still does not answer the core defect: the Final Rule’s redefinition of “frame or receiver” in § 921(a)(3)(B) effectively adds a “readily convertible receiver” category Congress did not enact, and we cannot save an ultra vires rule by hypothesizing alternative statutory hooks not reflected in the agency’s chosen definition. Justice Kagan’s gap-filling argument—because “frame or receiver” is undefined, ATF may draw a “readily” line—fails under my methodology where the line expands a criminally operative definition beyond the term’s ordinary public meaning at enactment; any genuine uncertainty is a reason for judicial restraint and, as Justice Thomas notes, triggers lenity rather than administrative creativity. Thompson/Center Arms, which Justice Sotomayor invokes, does not alter the analysis because it concerned how an aggregation of parts was treated under a different statutory/tax scheme and does not license an agency to redefine statutory terms in the GCA when Congress itself separated “weapon … readily convertible” from “frame or receiver.” I therefore remain with the Respondent: the Rule exceeds the statutory definition, and limiting constructions cannot cure that separation-of-powers problem.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas press the strongest objection: § 921(a)(3)(A)’s “may readily be converted” modifies “weapon,” not the distinct “frame or receiver” category in (B), and agencies cannot expand a criminal definition by adding a “readily convertible receiver” concept. But Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s narrower framing answers that critique by grounding coverage of integrated, marketed kits (and near-complete, functionally core housings) in (A)’s text—treating them as “weapons … designed to or may readily be converted,” rather than redefining (B) to sweep in any partial component. Thompson/Center Arms, as Justice Barrett and Justice Sotomayor note, supports looking to configuration and predictable intended use when parts are packaged to make the regulated end-state readily achievable, which mitigates the anti-evasion concern without adopting an unbounded “parts” theory. Given that textual hook and the practical administrability concerns, I do not see the “grievous ambiguity” required for lenity to control at this definitional stage, though our holding should be tightly limited to objective, readily completable kits/near-complete items.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas press the strongest textual point: § 921(a)(3)(A)’s “may readily be converted” modifies “weapon,” while § 921(a)(3)(B) separately lists “frame or receiver,” suggesting Congress drew a line at completed cores. But that separation does not defeat the government’s narrower path, emphasized by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito, that integrated kits and near-complete configurations can qualify as a “weapon … designed to or may readily be converted” under (A) without re-defining “frame or receiver” to include everything “close.” Thompson/Center Arms (as Justice Sotomayor notes) supports treating an aggregation of parts as the regulated object when its configuration makes the regulated end-state the predictable, intended use, which bolsters reading (A) to reach kits objectively packaged for prompt completion. Lenity, invoked by Justice Gorsuch, matters at the margins, but I do not see “grievous ambiguity” once (A)’s readily-convertible language is applied to coherent weapon-kits rather than remote components or raw materials.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest objection: § 921(a)(3)(B) lists “the frame or receiver” as a distinct category, and importing “readily convertible” risks agency enlargement of a criminal definition and triggers lenity. But Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan persuasively situate the Rule within § 921(a)(3) as an integrated definition—especially § 921(a)(3)(A)’s express “may readily be converted” language—which Congress used to prevent predictable evasion and which comfortably reaches objectively packaged, near-complete kits without authorizing a free-floating “parts” regime. Thompson/Center Arms, as Justice Sotomayor notes, reinforces looking to real-world configuration and intended, straightforward assembly when the regulated end-state is the practical and marketed use, which supports a narrow, administrable approval tethered to objective “readily” factors. Given this is a pre-enforcement APA case about statutory authorization (not a borderline prosecution), I do not see the “grievous ambiguity” needed to make lenity dispositive, though we should write narrowly to avoid sweeping in remote components.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Gun Control Act defines “firearm” to include a “frame or receiver,” 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3), and the government’s interpretation that certain near-complete frames/receivers and closely integrated kits can qualify when they are functionally equivalent and readily completed is at least a permissible reading in light of longstanding ATF administration and the statute’s evident regulatory design. A narrow disposition preserving the core of the Final Rule avoids a sweeping holding that would destabilize settled regulatory practice and undermine institutional legitimacy, while leaving for another day any application to more remote, early-stage components. Procedurally, our interim stay order’s limiting language (“insofar as”) is best read to stay only the district court’s vacatur remedy under APA § 706(2), thereby maintaining the status quo pending review without resolving the broader merits. This approach is consistent with the Court’s careful use of emergency relief in analogous contexts, e.g., Danco Laboratories, LLC v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 143 S. Ct. 1075 (2023) (mem.).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Gun Control Act defines “firearm” to include “the frame or receiver of any such weapon,” 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3)(B), and the ordinary public meaning of “frame” and “receiver” at enactment refers to the basic structural unit of a firearm—not an item that is merely “partially complete” or a “parts kit” that may later be made into one. ATF’s Final Rule effectively adds a “readily convertible” concept Congress did not enact, expanding criminally significant coverage beyond the statute’s text, and thus is “not in accordance with law” and must be set aside under the APA, 5 U.S.C. § 706(2). Procedurally, the Court’s interim stay—by its limiting language (“insofar as”)—should be read to suspend only the vacatur remedy, not to rewrite or nullify the rest of the district court’s judgment. The government’s position invites agencies to cure statutory gaps by regulation, contrary to textual limits and the Constitution’s separation of powers.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Gun Control Act defines a “firearm” to include “any weapon … which will or is designed to or may readily be converted to expel a projectile,” 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3)(A), and that text comfortably reaches weapon-parts kits that are sold in a configuration that can “readily be converted” into an operable gun. By contrast, a categorical rule excluding partially complete components and kits would invite obvious evasion and undermine practical enforcement of Congress’s scheme, while the Rule can be understood as implementing, not rewriting, the statutory phrase “readily be converted.” As to procedure, the Court’s interim stay “insofar as” it vacated the Rule is best read to halt the district court’s judgment to that extent, preserving the Rule’s operation pending review rather than allowing vacatur to take effect through artful remedial framing. In this posture, I would favor an interpretation that maintains uniform federal enforceability and avoids disrupting ongoing criminal and regulatory reliance interests while the merits are resolved.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Gun Control Act’s definition of “firearm” reaches not only weapons that “will” expel a projectile but those “designed to” or that “may readily be converted” to do so, 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3), and that language is best read to allow ATF to address near-complete frames/receivers and kits that are functionally firearms-in-waiting, given the statute’s preventive purpose and real-world consequences for public safety. Thompson/Center Arms supports treating certain aggregations of parts as a regulated firearm when, in practical terms, they are configured and marketed so that conversion to a functioning gun is straightforward rather than speculative. Under the APA, courts may “set aside” unlawful agency action, 5 U.S.C. § 706(2), but remedial tailoring matters; and the Supreme Court’s interim stay “insofar as” the judgment vacated the Rule is most naturally read to halt the vacatur remedy while leaving other aspects of the judgment undisturbed. A narrower, impacts-sensitive approach avoids creating a regulatory gap that disproportionately endangers vulnerable communities while merits review proceeds.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 921(a)(3) defines “firearm” to include not only a weapon that fires, but also one “designed to” do so or that “may readily be converted” to do so, and it separately includes “the frame or receiver of any such weapon”; read together, that structure supports ATF’s authority to regulate items that are functionally equivalent to, or readily convertible into, a frame/receiver when sold in configurations (including kits) that make completion straightforward and predictable. Because Congress did not define “frame or receiver,” the agency may fill that gap with a workable, technology-responsive line so long as it remains tethered to the statute’s text and purpose, and the Rule’s focus on objective “readily” factors fits the GCA’s broader design to control commerce in firearms rather than allow easy evasion through near-complete components. On the procedural question, the Court’s stay order in VanDerStok, by its limiting “insofar as” formulation, is best read to halt the district court’s judgment only to the extent it vacated the rule, leaving other aspects of the judgment undisturbed. That reading respects ordinary remedial principles under the APA (5 U.S.C. §§ 706(2), 705) and avoids overbroad interim relief not clearly granted by the Court.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 921(a)(3) defines a “firearm” to include a weapon that “will or is designed to or may readily be converted” to expel a projectile, but separately lists “the frame or receiver of any such weapon,” and that textual separation suggests Congress meant a completed frame/receiver—not any “partially complete, disassembled, or nonfunctional” item or a parts kit—as a standalone regulated “firearm.” Because Congress did not define “frame or receiver,” we apply the ordinary public meaning at enactment, and the ATF may not expand that meaning by regulation when the statute’s words do not bear it; the “major questions”/separation-of-powers concern is that an agency cannot assume power to rewrite core statutory definitions. Given the resulting criminal and compliance consequences, any lingering ambiguity should be resolved against the government under the rule of lenity, reinforcing that the Final Rule exceeds ATF’s authority under the APA, 5 U.S.C. § 706(2). Procedurally, the Court’s stay “insofar as” the judgment vacated the Rule should be read narrowly to halt only that vacatur remedy, not to suspend other portions of the district court’s judgment beyond the vacatur itself.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the Gun Control Act’s text and long historical practice, ATF may treat certain partially complete frames/receivers and kits as “firearms” when they are readily convertible to functional frames/receivers, a practical and workable interpretation consistent with § 921(a)(3)’s inclusion of “frame or receiver” and Congress’s evident purpose to regulate the core regulated item rather than invite easy evasion through minor incompleteness. This case does not present the kind of transformative assertion of power that would trigger the “clear congressional authorization” demand of West Virginia v. EPA, 142 S. Ct. 2587 (2022); it is an implementation detail within ATF’s traditional wheelhouse, and reading the statute to categorically exclude near-complete receivers would create serious administrability and enforcement problems. Procedurally, the Court’s interim stay, phrased to apply “insofar as” the district court vacated the rule, should be read narrowly to preserve only the rule’s operative effect pending review and not to freeze all other aspects of the district court’s judgment beyond the vacatur remedy, consistent with ordinary remedial principles under the APA, 5 U.S.C. § 706(2), and the limited nature of stays. Given the institutional costs of destabilizing a nationwide regulatory regime on a cramped reading, I would reverse the judgment invalidating the rule (at least as applied to readily convertible components/kits) while maintaining a restrained, text-and-tradition grounded approach to the remedial question.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Gun Control Act defines “firearm” to include not only an operable weapon but also any weapon “designed to or may readily be converted” to expel a projectile, 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3)(A), and separately includes “the frame or receiver of any such weapon,” § 921(a)(3)(B). Read in context and according to ordinary public meaning, “frame or receiver” need not be limited to fully complete, functional housings if the item sold is, in substance, the core firearm component that is readily finishable for that purpose; likewise, kits can fall within § 921(a)(3)(A) when their design and composition make them readily convertible into an operable weapon. On the procedural question, the Court’s interim stay “insofar as” it vacated the rule (Garland v. VanDerStok, 2023 WL 5023383 (mem.)) is best read to halt the district court’s judgment only to that extent, preserving other aspects of the judgment not dependent on vacatur. Given the statutory text and the limited scope of the stay language, I would reverse the Fifth Circuit’s cramped reading and uphold the Rule at least as applied to readily convertible kits and near-complete frames/receivers consistent with § 921(a)(3).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under the Gun Control Act’s functional terms, including “frame or receiver,” 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3), ATF has room to treat certain kits and partially complete components as regulated when they are readily convertible into the core housing that makes a firearm traceable, and the APA does not require a hyper-literal reading that defeats the statute’s practical aims. Given the real-world consequences for enforcement and public safety, a construction that allows regulation of near-complete, easily finished components better serves Congress’s evident purpose while still preserving notice-and-comment constraints. Procedurally, the Court’s interim stay “insofar as” the judgment vacated the rule is best read as a limited stay of the APA vacatur remedy—not a blanket suspension of every aspect of the district court’s judgment—consistent with the ordinary meaning of “insofar as” and the Court’s contrasting use of an unqualified stay in Danco Laboratories (2023) (mem.). Because vacatur operates by nullifying the rule’s legal effect rather than commanding affirmative conduct, staying the vacatur appropriately preserves the regulatory status quo pending review without implicitly wiping out other, non-vacatur relief.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the ATF’s 2022–2023 “frame or receiver/ghost gun” Final Rule lawfully interprets and applies the Gun Control Act’s definition of “firearm” to weapon-parts kits and partially complete frames/receivers, and—procedurally—what the Supreme Court’s stay order means by staying the lower-court judgments only “insofar as” they vacated the rule.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Gun Control Act of 1968 (18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3) and related provisions defining “firearm,” “frame or receiver,” and regulating firearm sales/serialization), and the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 706 (judicial review; remedies including vacatur)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The government (Garland/DOJ/ATF) argues that the Final Rule is a permissible construction of the Gun Control Act because the statute can reasonably cover at least some partially complete frames/receivers and weapon-parts kits that are designed to be readily converted into functional firearms; the rule closes an enforcement gap exploited by “ghost gun” sellers while staying within statutory bounds and traditional agency interpretive authority. In the procedural posture reflected in the excerpts, petitioners also urged the Supreme Court to stay the district court’s judgment and, at minimum, to prevent the district court’s APA vacatur from operating beyond the parties—hence the Supreme Court’s stay “insofar as” the judgments vacated the rule.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The challengers (VanDerStok et al.) contend that the Gun Control Act regulates completed firearms (and true frames/receivers), not unfinished components or aggregations of parts sold as kits; they argue ATF exceeded its statutory authority by effectively rewriting the statute to reach items Congress did not regulate. As to remedy/procedure, respondents have treated the district court’s vacatur as invalidating the Final Rule broadly, while the quoted lower-court discussion emphasizes that the Supreme Court’s stay language (“insofar as”) indicates only a partial stay—targeting the vacatur remedy rather than staying every aspect of the district court’s orders.
key_precedents: Garland v. VanDerStok, No. 23A82, 2023 WL 5023383 (U.S. Aug. 8, 2023) (mem.)
Morrison v. Olson, 484 U.S. 1058 (1988) (stay order referencing “full stay”)
Danco Laboratories, LLC v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 143 S. Ct. 1075 (2023) (mem.)
Pub. Serv. Co. of Ind. v. EPA, 682 F.2d 626, 635 n.15 (7th Cir. 1982)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s expressio unius point remains the strongest objection, and I agree with him and Justice Gorsuch that we cannot simply read “may readily be converted” into § 921(a)(3)(B) or let an agency redefine an unfinished object as “the frame or receiver” Congress specified. But Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan persuasively show that (B)’s “of any such weapon” is a genuine cross-reference to the weapon category defined in (A), allowing a narrow holding that upholds application to commercial kit configurations that, as sold, are objectively “designed to” and “may readily be converted” into a firearm under (A), while rejecting the Rule’s outermost applications that sweep in items not yet a frame/receiver in ordinary terms. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity and separation-of-powers concerns reinforce (rather than defeat) that minimalist approach: we should require clear, readily-convertible facts and avoid endorsing vague, discretionary multi-factor expansions with criminal consequences. The Utility Air/West Virginia major-questions cautions (raised by Justices Alito and Thomas) support careful tailoring, but here the government’s best case rests on the statute’s own enacted “readily convertible” language in (A), not an agency-discovered power in a peripheral provision.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest point from the other side is Justice Kagan’s (and the Chief Justice’s) claim that (B)’s “of any such weapon” cross-reference pulls in (A)’s “designed to”/“may readily be converted” concepts, permitting regulation of kits through (B). But textually and in original public meaning, that phrase does not rewrite the object of (B)—“the frame or receiver”—into “something that may readily become a frame or receiver”; it merely identifies whose frame/receiver (i.e., of a firearm described in (A)) is covered. Chief Justice Roberts’ proposed narrow path under (A) may address some kits, but it cannot salvage the Rule’s central move of treating unfinished blocks and partial assemblies as the completed “frame or receiver” Congress specified in (B), especially where criminal exposure turns on an agency’s multi-factor test; Justice Gorsuch’s lenity/separation-of-powers concern therefore remains dispositive for the Rule’s expansion. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Pub. Serv. Co. of Ind. v. EPA and the Court’s “insofar as” stay language speaks to remedy and does not supply the missing statutory authorization on the merits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s cross-reference theory (“frame or receiver of any such weapon”) does not overcome the deliberate textual choice Congress made to place “may readily be converted” in § 921(a)(3)(A) and omit it from (B); as Justice Thomas explains, the cross-reference identifies the kind of weapon whose frame/receiver is regulated, it does not redefine unfinished objects into “the frame or receiver.” Even accepting Justice Kavanaugh’s point that some kits can be treated as “weapons” under (A), the Rule’s core expansion still turns on treating incomplete blocks and multi-part assemblies as “frames or receivers,” a move with criminal consequences that triggers Justice Gorsuch’s lenity and separation-of-powers concerns. Nor do the workability/evasion considerations or historical enforcement practice supply authority Congress withheld, and Utility Air/West Virginia caution against locating sweeping, criminally enforceable power in definitional provisions absent clear statutory text. The stay’s “insofar as” language, as Roberts and Sotomayor note, is remedial and does not cure the merits defect in the Rule’s redefinition.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest objection: Congress placed “may readily be converted” in § 921(a)(3)(A) but not in (B), so ATF cannot treat unfinished items as “the frame or receiver.” I agree that point blocks any boundless redefinition of (B), but it does not defeat the government’s narrower theory—endorsed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett—that many commercial kits, as sold and marketed, qualify as “weapons” under (A) because they are designed to and may readily be converted, and (B) then applies only to sufficiently complete items that are already a frame/receiver in ordinary terms “of any such weapon.” Utility Air and West Virginia (raised by Justice Alito) do not move me because ATF is working within the GCA’s core definitional/serialization scheme rather than claiming transformative new regulatory power from a peripheral provision. Lenity (Justice Gorsuch) reinforces that our holding should be cabined and as-applied to clearly readily-convertible configurations, but it does not compel invalidation where the statutory text supplies workable notice and limiting principles for the core conduct at issue.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s expressio unius point remains the strongest textual objection, and I agree with him (and Justice Gorsuch) that we cannot simply “import” the word “readily” from § 921(a)(3)(A) into (B) to transform incomplete blocks into “the frame or receiver.” But I also think the Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s narrower route answers that objection on its own terms: many commercial “kits,” as sold and marketed, fit comfortably within (A)’s enacted phrase “designed to” and “may readily be converted,” and then (B)’s “frame or receiver of any such weapon” operates only for items that are, in ordinary usage, already frames/receivers. Justice Alito’s Utility Air/West Virginia caution is a useful reminder to avoid agency-freewheeling, yet those cases are less apt where Congress itself supplied the operative limiting language (“readily be converted”) and we confine the holding to core, objectively readily-convertible configurations rather than validating the Rule’s outer margins. Lenity (Justice Gorsuch) may still matter for borderline applications, which is exactly why an as-applied, cabined disposition is the correct solution rather than categorical invalidation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I take seriously the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s effort to salvage a narrow disposition by relying principally on § 921(a)(3)(A) for “readily convertible” kits while confining (B) to sufficiently complete receivers. But even on that approach, the government’s position in this case remains bound up with treating incomplete objects as “the frame or receiver” under (B), and the cross-reference “of any such weapon” does not, in ordinary 1968 usage, authorize reclassifying non-frames as frames; it merely identifies whose frame/receiver counts, not what counts as a frame/receiver. Justice Barrett and Justice Sotomayor are right that lenity comes late, yet here the statutory structure—Congress’s deliberate placement of “readily” in (A) but not (B), as Justice Thomas stresses—creates the kind of boundary-drawing ambiguity that an agency should not resolve in a criminally enforceable way. Justice Kavanaugh’s appeal to historical enforcement practice cannot enlarge the enacted definition, and the stay’s “insofar as” language (as Roberts/Sotomayor note) is remedial and cannot supply missing statutory authorization.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest point: Congress put “may readily be converted” in § 921(a)(3)(A) but not in (B), so we cannot rewrite (B) to reach any unfinished object an agency thinks is close enough. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts’s narrower approach that the government need not win by importing “readily” into (B): the core kit cases can be sustained under (A) where, as sold and marketed, the configuration is objectively designed to and may readily be converted into a functioning firearm, while (B) should be limited to items that are, in ordinary terms, already a frame or receiver (not mere blocks or vague multi-factor near-misses). Justice Gorsuch’s lenity/separation-of-powers concerns are a real constraint at the margins and counsel against blessing the Rule’s outer applications, but they do not require categorical invalidation where (A)’s enacted “readily convertible” language supplies a clear limiting principle and fair-notice anchor. Justice Alito’s major-questions framing does not move me because this is the definitional core Congress addressed in the GCA, and our holding can be expressly cabined to avoid any agency-driven expansion beyond the statute’s text.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s expressio unius point remains the most serious textual objection: Congress said “may readily be converted” in § 921(a)(3)(A) but not in (B), and we should not redefine an unfinished block as “the frame or receiver” Congress specified. But I agree with Justice Kagan (and the Chief) that (B)’s phrase “of any such weapon” is not surplusage; it is a cross-reference that ties the regulated frame/receiver to the statute’s weapon-category in (A), so the Rule is at least valid as applied to kits that, as sold, are objectively “designed to” and “may readily be converted” into firearms, while (B) can be confined to sufficiently complete items that are already frames/receivers in ordinary usage. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity concern underscores the need to reject the Rule’s outermost applications and vague multi-factor discretion, but lenity does not override the statute’s ordinary textual link between (A) and (B) where the core “readily convertible kit” applications are not grievously ambiguous. I do not read Utility Air/West Virginia (as Justice Alito invokes them) to control here because the authority comes from the GCA’s central definitional text itself, and our holding can be cabined to avoid any agency “discovery” of new power at the margins.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas (and Justice Gorsuch) press the strongest point: Congress put “may readily be converted” in § 921(a)(3)(A) but not in (B), so we should not redefine unfinished blocks as “the frame or receiver” and thereby expand criminal liability by agency say-so. I agree with that caution and, with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan, I think it is answered by deciding the case principally under (A): many commercial “kits,” as marketed and packaged, are plausibly “weapons” because they are designed to and may readily be converted into firearms, while (B) is limited to sufficiently complete items that are already, in ordinary terms, frames/receivers of such weapons. That approach respects Thomas’s expressio-unius concern (no importing “readily” into (B)) while addressing Gorsuch’s fair-notice/lenity worry by anchoring liability to clear “readily convertible” facts and rejecting the Rule’s vague outer margins. Justice Alito’s major-questions/Utility Air–West Virginia framing does not move me here because, on this narrowed view, ATF is not discovering vast new authority but applying the GCA’s core definitional text to an obvious evasion channel, and the stay’s “insofar as” language (as Roberts/Sotomayor note) supports a restrained remedy-focused disposition rather than a sweeping merits pronouncement.

John Roberts.reasoning: Given the stay’s text—granting relief only “insofar as” the lower-court judgments vacated the Final Rule—the better reading is a partial stay aimed at restoring the rule’s operative effect while leaving other aspects of the district court’s orders intact, consistent with the Court’s remedial practice in emergency applications. On the merits, I would proceed narrowly: the Gun Control Act’s definition of “firearm” includes the “frame or receiver,” 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3), and ATF has at least some room to interpret that term to reach items designed to be “readily” converted into functioning frames/receivers and firearms, without adopting the lower court’s broad conclusion that Congress “clearly and without question” foreclosed any regulation of partially complete frames/receivers. The major-questions framework of West Virginia v. EPA cautions against transformative assertions of agency power absent clear authorization, but this rule operates within a long-regulated domain (firearm serialization and commercial distribution) and can be sustained in a limited set of applications without endorsing the agency’s outermost claims. A restrained disposition would preserve institutional legitimacy by avoiding an unnecessarily sweeping invalidation and by resolving the case on statutory and remedial grounds under the GCA and APA, 5 U.S.C. § 706, rather than reaching broader constitutional issues.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Gun Control Act defines “firearm” to include “(A) any weapon … which will or is designed to or may readily be converted to expel a projectile” and separately “(B) the frame or receiver of any such weapon,” 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3), but it does not extend “readily converted” language to “frame or receiver.” Under a textualist reading, that deliberate inclusion in (A) and omission in (B) forecloses ATF’s effort to treat partially complete items and parts kits as “frames or receivers,” because an agency may not “rewrite” statutory terms to close perceived gaps. The Supreme Court’s stay “insofar as” the judgments vacated the rule indicates a limited stay of the vacatur remedy under APA review (5 U.S.C. § 706) rather than an endorsement of the Rule’s legality. Following the ordinary-meaning canon as in Germain v. United States, 503 U.S. 249, 254 (1992), the statute’s text controls over policy arguments about enforcement needs.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Gun Control Act’s definition of “firearm” in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3) most naturally covers completed weapons and the actual “frame or receiver,” not unfinished components or aggregations of parts sold as kits; ATF’s Final Rule stretches those terms beyond their ordinary 1968 meaning, contrary to the textualist approach emphasized in New Prime Inc. v. Oliveira. Given the Rule’s sweeping practical effect—expanding federal serialization and background-check obligations to a broad, new category of items—this is the sort of policy decision requiring clear congressional authorization, not agency revision, under West Virginia v. EPA and Utility Air Regulatory Group v. EPA. While the public-safety and law-enforcement interests are substantial, the APA cannot be used to ratify an agency rewriting statutory limits, and Congress remains free to amend the GCA if it wishes to reach “ghost gun” kits. Procedurally, the Court’s stay “insofar as” the judgments vacated the Rule indicates only that the nationwide vacatur remedy was stayed, not that the Rule was definitively lawful on the merits.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Gun Control Act defines “firearm” to include a “frame or receiver,” 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3), and ATF’s rule reasonably applies that definition to items designed and marketed to be readily converted into functioning guns, addressing a real enforcement gap that disproportionately harms communities vulnerable to gun violence. On the procedural question, the Supreme Court’s stay “insofar as” the judgments vacated the rule is best read, consistent with ordinary legal usage and the lower-court reliance on Black’s and Pub. Serv. Co. of Ind. v. EPA, as a partial stay limited to the APA vacatur remedy rather than a wholesale suspension of all aspects of the judgments. The APA directs courts to “hold unlawful and set aside” agency action found unlawful, 5 U.S.C. § 706(2), but the Court’s calibrated stay language indicates it intended to prevent broad vacatur from taking effect while merits review proceeds, much as the Court has managed remedial scope through stay orders in cases like Danco Laboratories (mem.). Given the practical stakes for public safety and access to justice, and the statute’s text leaving room for this application, I would vote to uphold the rule at least as applied to readily convertible kits and partially complete frames/receivers.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3)(A), Congress defined “firearm” to include not only a weapon that “will” fire, but one that “is designed to or may readily be converted” to do so, and § 921(a)(3)(B) separately reaches “the frame or receiver of any such weapon”—text that sensibly accommodates at least some partially complete frames/receivers and certain kits sold in a configuration designed for ready conversion. Reading the statute to categorically exclude such items risks undermining the GCA’s coherent regulatory scheme (serialization, background checks) by turning on easily manipulated manufacturing and packaging steps, and the Final Rule’s “readily” factors operate as a workability constraint rather than an open-ended expansion. This is not a “major questions” style rewriting of the statute; unlike Utility Air Regulatory Group v. EPA, the agency here is applying Congress’s own “readily be converted” language to modern evasion tactics rather than claiming newfound power from a peripheral provision. Procedurally, the Court’s stay “insofar as” the judgments vacated the rule is best read to suspend the vacatur remedy under APA § 706 while leaving other aspects of the lower-court rulings untouched, preserving nationwide regulatory continuity pending review.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under the Gun Control Act, a “firearm” includes “any weapon … which will or is designed to or may readily be converted to expel a projectile” and “the frame or receiver of any such weapon,” 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3); reading those terms in their ordinary meaning at enactment, a collection of parts or an unfinished blank that is not yet a “weapon” and not yet a true “frame or receiver” falls outside the statute. The Final Rule’s effort to treat weapon-parts “kits” and partially complete components as regulated “firearms” or “frames or receivers” effectively expands criminally enforceable obligations without clear congressional authorization, raising separation-of-powers concerns and triggering the clear-statement principle reflected in West Virginia v. EPA, 142 S. Ct. 2587, 2614 (2022). Where the statutory text does not clearly reach the challenged items, the rule of lenity counsels against adopting an agency interpretation that enlarges criminal exposure. Procedurally, the Supreme Court’s stay “insofar as” the judgments vacated the Rule indicates a limited stay of the vacatur remedy (under APA § 706) rather than a wholesale stay of every aspect of the lower-court orders, but that clarification does not supply the missing statutory authority for the Rule’s core expansion.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Gun Control Act’s definition of “firearm” reaches not only a fully operable weapon but also items “designed to” or that “may readily be converted” to expel a projectile, 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3)(A), and separately regulates “the frame or receiver,” § 921(a)(3)(B); history and longstanding enforcement practice support treating sufficiently complete frames/receivers and near-complete kits as within those terms when they are readily convertible. The challengers’ major-questions framing is a poor fit here: the Final Rule addresses a traditional subject (firearms commerce and serialization) rather than an agency’s assertion of broad new regulatory power of the kind at issue in West Virginia v. EPA, 142 S. Ct. 2587 (2022). Practically, the “readily convertible” line-drawing is workable and consistent with prior applications to incomplete firearms (e.g., United States v. Ryles, 988 F.2d 13 (5th Cir. 1993)), whereas categorically excluding kits would create an obvious evasion of Congress’s scheme. Procedurally, the Supreme Court’s stay “insofar as” the judgments vacated the rule indicates a partial stay directed at the remedy of nationwide vacatur under the APA (5 U.S.C. § 706), leaving other aspects of the lower-court orders undisturbed while appellate review proceeds (cf. Danco Labs., LLC v. Alliance for Hippocratic Med., 143 S. Ct. 1075 (2023) (mem.)).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Gun Control Act defines “firearm” to include “any weapon … which will or is designed to or may readily be converted to expel a projectile,” as well as “the frame or receiver of any such weapon,” 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3)(A), (B). Read in light of ordinary meaning and the statute’s cross-reference (“any such weapon”), that text can encompass at least those weapon-parts kits and partially complete frames/receivers that are objectively designed to, and may readily be converted into, an operable weapon or its frame/receiver—so the Rule is not facially beyond the statute’s original public meaning. Procedurally, the Court’s stay “insofar as” the judgments vacated the Rule most naturally operates as a partial stay directed at the remedial vacatur under the APA (5 U.S.C. § 706), leaving other aspects of the lower-court orders intact while preventing the Rule from being nullified pending review. The stay order in Garland v. VanDerStok is therefore best read to halt only the vacatur’s effect, consistent with the Court’s practice of tailoring stays to specific portions of judgments.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 921(a)(3) defines “firearm” to include a “weapon … which will or is designed to or may readily be converted” to expel a projectile, and ATF reasonably construed that text—together with the statute’s inclusion of the “frame or receiver” (§ 921(a)(3)(B))—to reach at least some weapon-parts kits and partially complete frames/receivers that are marketed and sold as readily convertible firearms, a construction with substantial practical consequences for traceability and public safety. Under the APA, the district court’s chosen remedy of nationwide vacatur is distinct from party-specific relief, and the Supreme Court’s stay “insofar as” the judgments vacated the rule is best read as a targeted stay of that vacatur remedy “to the degree or extent” it nullified the rule beyond the parties. That reading tracks ordinary legal usage of “insofar as” (as noted in Pub. Serv. Co. of Ind. v. EPA) and contrasts with orders expressly granting a “full stay” (Morrison v. Olson) or staying an entire order without limitation (Danco Laboratories). Given the procedural posture and the need for administrable, fair enforcement, I would uphold the government’s position at least as to the permissibility of applying the Rule to readily convertible kits/unfinished receivers and the limited scope of the stay.
